title: Sampling, Laboratory Results and Data Quality
audience: Practising drinking-water operators and supervisors seeking focused applied development.
prerequisites: Basic operator terminology, metric calculations and access to the source readings. Use a calculator; all supplied facility data are fictional.
introduction: Build a sampling and result-review package for a fictional reservoir investigation. Practise representativeness, traceability, quality-control interpretation and qualified reporting.
delivery: Facilitated pilot with four practical modules, source reading, instructor discussion, a final assessment and evaluation. Breaks are excluded. Planned duration requires a timed pilot; no approved CEUs are awarded.

modules.title: Design a sample that answers the question
objectives: Align location and timing with a stated decision.
Distinguish independent sampling from repeat analysis.
modules.lesson:
### Define the decision first
“Take more samples” is not a sampling plan. State the question, decision boundary, locations, times, sample types, analytical method and responsibilities. A sample at a treatment outlet answers a different question from one at a distant reservoir outlet. Repeated measurements of one bottle describe analytical repeatability; they do not create independent evidence about spatial variability.

Suppose a reservoir outlet has a low-residual complaint at 07:00. A treatment-plant grab at 14:00 cannot establish the reservoir condition at 07:00. It may still help characterize the source feeding the system. Pairing time-stamped upstream and downstream observations, with travel-time and mixing limitations documented, is more informative than treating two unrelated grabs as the same water parcel.

A field duplicate is collected to examine variability introduced by sampling and measurement under the stated procedure. A laboratory duplicate examines a different part of the measurement chain. Neither automatically proves that the sample represented the whole system. Document whether samples were sequential, split or independently collected.

Required compliance sampling remains governed by the applicable current requirements and approved sampling arrangements. The investigation in this lesson is supplemental and cannot silently replace them. Use the source to identify handling and quality controls, then record the locally applicable method rather than inventing a universal holding time.
modules.evidence:
**Reservoir investigation Q1**
Complaint at outletR2 at 07:00. SourceS1 is 4 km upstream. Approximate travel time varies 2–6 hours; the reservoir mixes inflow with stored water. Existing required samples remain scheduled under the facility plan.

| Proposal | Sampling |
|---|---|
| A | Five repeat readings of one S1 bottle at 14:00 |
| B | R2 observations at 06:30,07:00,07:30 plus paired S1 observations and operating records |
| C | One R2 sample next Friday at noon |

Q2: The question is whether recurrent early-morning outlet conditions coincide with a particular reservoir operating state, not whether one bottle can be measured precisely.
modules.assignment: Draft a 350–500-word supplemental sampling plan. Select and improve one proposal; justify locations and times; specify independent sampling versus repeat readings, chain-of-custody responsibilities and records of reservoir operation. Explain two limits on interpreting “paired” samples and how required sampling is preserved.
rubric: Distinguishes spatial evidence from repeat measurement.
Preserves required sampling and names method/handling verification.
modules.facilitatorGuide: B best addresses the recurrent time window, but not conclusively after one morning. Strong plans repeat across relevant operating states and document levels, inflow/outflow and sampling methods. A measures one bottle repeatedly; C misses the stated window. Do not accept 2–6 hours as an exact lag or a claim that S1/R2 samples are necessarily the same parcel. Require independent observations and local method verification.

modules.title: Trace samples and preserve corrections
objectives: Resolve conflicting identifiers without overwriting originals.
modules.lesson:
### The result must remain connected to the sample
Traceability links the sampling plan, field identifier, bottle, custody record, laboratory accession and reported result. A mismatch can break that chain even when the numerical analysis is correct. Resolve it through documented evidence; do not choose the most convenient location and rewrite the original record.

A useful correction preserves the original entry, identifies who corrected it and when, states the reason and cites supporting evidence. A field recollection made later is weaker than a contemporaneous location scan, but it may still be relevant. Record uncertainty when evidence is insufficient. The laboratory controls its own report amendments; the operator should request clarification through the approved channel rather than edit a laboratory PDF.

Elapsed time is calculated from actual collection to the required event, using the method-specific rule. Receipt and analysis are different events. A sample received promptly may still be analysed late. Conversely, a transcription error in a receipt time requires investigation before declaring the sample invalid. Preserve the dates and time zones, especially across midnight.

Where a result triggers a protective or reporting response, an identifier discrepancy does not itself cancel the applicable obligation. Follow the current procedure while resolving identity. This lesson supplies no universal preservation, temperature or holding-time requirement: those come from the applicable method and laboratory instructions.
modules.evidence:
**Q3 — custody records**
Bottle label R2-091, collection September 12 at 23:40. Field form saysR2; barcode location scan at 23:39 saysR2. Custody destination line saysR7. Courier collection September 13 at 00:10; laboratory receipt 01:25; analysis begins 08:05. Laboratory accessionL491 referencesR2-091 but report locationR7.

Q4: Technician writes at 10:00, “I believe I copied yesterday’s R7 line.” The laboratory has not issued an amended report. No method-specific holding-time limit is supplied.
modules.assignment: Prepare a timeline with elapsed collection-to-receipt and collection-to-analysis times. Draft a correction request that preserves both conflicting location entries, cites evidence and asks the laboratory to confirm the mapping. State what is known, what remains unconfirmed and what information is required before deciding whether the timing meets the method.
rubric: Preserves original IDs and routes report amendment appropriately.
Does not infer a method limit or cancel a response automatically.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Receipt elapsed 1 h 45 m; analysis 8 h 25 m. Contemporary barcode and form supportR2; the lab report remainsR7 until clarified. Require an auditable amendment request, not an editedPDF or assertion of validity. The analyst must obtain the applicable method limit and event definition; neither elapsed time alone proves acceptable handling. Discuss how urgent reporting and identity resolution can proceed together.

modules.title: Interpret blanks, duplicates and reporting limits
objectives: Separate contamination evidence from sample representativeness.
modules.lesson:
### Quality controls diagnose parts of the chain
A blank can reveal contamination introduced by materials, transport, handling or analysis, depending on how that blank was prepared. It cannot identify the source by itself. A field blank and laboratory blank cover different processes. Investigate the relevant chain rather than subtracting a blank result from every sample without an approved method.

Relative percent difference (RPD) is **absolute difference ÷ pair mean ×100**. Results 0.40 and 0.50 mg/L have a mean 0.45 and RPD22.2%. Their absolute difference is 0.10 mg/L. Close to a method's reporting limit, a small absolute difference may create a large percentage; interpretation requires the method's criteria, concentration range and sample matrix.

For this exercise only, the fictional duplicate rule is RPD≤20% when both results are at least 0.20 mg/L; below that range, the method uses a separate absolute-difference rule that is not supplied. Do not export this rule to real operations. A failed duplicate criterion calls for documented review; it does not automatically identify which result is wrong.

A “less than” result is censored information, not a zero and not an exact value at the limit. Keep that notation in the dataset. If a calculation requires substitution, the authorized analytical plan must define and disclose it. Never silently replace qualified data to make a trend look cleaner.
modules.evidence:
**Q5 — fictional analytical batch**
| Pair | Results mg/L | Other evidence |
|---|---|---|
| D1 |0.40,0.50|Same field-duplicate procedure |
| D2 |0.03,0.05|Both below 0.20 applicability boundary |
| B1 field blank |0.04|Lab blank<0.01 |
| S1 sample |<0.02|Reporting limit 0.02 |

The 20% criterion applies only under the condition in the lesson. The low-range criterion and blank-action rule must be requested from the laboratory.
modules.assignment: Calculate D1 and D2 RPD and absolute differences. Prepare a qualified batch review: apply the supplied rule only where valid, state what the blank comparison suggests without assigning a source, and preserve S1's reporting notation. Draft three precise questions to the laboratory that would resolve the missing criteria.
rubric: Correct RPD values and applicability boundary.
Does not subtract the blank or select a “true” duplicate result.
Retains censored notation and identifies missing rules.
modules.facilitatorGuide: D1RPD22.22%, difference 0.10: fails supplied 20% criterion. D2 mean 0.04,RPD50%,difference 0.02; no accept/reject conclusion under the unavailable low-range rule. Field blank detection with lab blank below 0.01 points to investigation beyond laboratory blank contamination, not proof of a specific field source. S1 mustremain<0.02. Return categorical acceptance/rejection unsupported by criteria.

modules.title: Write a decision-ready result summary
objectives: Separate findings, limitations and next actions.
Prevent unsupported claims from entering a public summary.
modules.lesson:
### Report what the evidence can support
A result summary should answer the operational question and show the strength of that answer. Organize it into findings, limitations, actions and owners. Keep raw evidence identifiers beside conclusions so a reviewer can reconstruct the reasoning.

A useful statement is specific: “AtR2 on three mornings, the low-residual observations occurred during the recorded low-turnover state; other operating states have not yet been sampled.” It is stronger than “water age caused the problem,” because the latter claims a mechanism not isolated by the data. Association can guide the next investigation without becoming a causal conclusion.

Separate analytical qualifications from operational risk. A custody discrepancy, blank detection or duplicate concern may limit interpretation while an operating condition still requires response. Escalate through the current procedure and state the evidence gap. Do not call water safe, unsafe or compliant solely from the narrow fictional dataset.

The final report must also be usable by the next shift. Assign each unresolved question to a role, specify the expected evidence and give a follow-up time or event. In the instructor discussion, explain what new evidence would reverse your leading interpretation. Revise the report to reflect the critique rather than adding a generic disclaimer.
modules.evidence:
**Q6 — proposed management statement**
“Five tests prove the entire reservoir is stable. The laboratory’s R7 label is a typo, so we corrected the PDF. The blank was only 0.04, which we subtracted. All samples meet holding time. No follow-up is needed.”

UseQ1–Q5. No additional sampling has occurred; no amended laboratory report or method-specific timing rule has arrived. Operations requests a defensible one-page status update.
modules.assignment: Replace Q6 with a 450–650-word decision memo. Reference at least five evidence IDs or records, include a limitations table and a follow-up register with owners. Explain each removed claim and propose a targeted next sampling round. Present the memo to the instructor, revise it and complete the final assessment and evaluation.
rubric: Corrects all five unsupported claims in Q6.
Uses a clear evidence trail and specific follow-up requests.
Keeps operational response and analytical review connected without declaring compliance.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Expected corrections: five repeat readings are not system coverage;R7 amendment is pending;blank subtraction is unsupported;holding-time rule missing;follow-up remains needed. Accept concise tables within the word target. Ask learner which missing evidence most changes the operational decision. Return any memo quietly retaining an edited lab report or blanket safety statement. Final assessment and evaluation fit the revised last-module timetable.
